analysis:
This batch contains only documentation: a new changelog fragment (changelog.d/provider-update-rollback.md, lines 1-7) and an operations doc edit (docs/operations/provider-release.md, date bump at line 3 and a new paragraph in head at ~1033-1040). No executable code, workflow or policy changes are in the supplied evidence, so no concrete regression can be cited.

The docs describe a new `darkbloom update --rollback` capability. The documented claims are: it keeps one earlier signed release; verifies that release's hash and signature before restoring it; runs the swap in the watchdog's journaled swap under the update lease; contacts no coordinator; quarantines the rolled-back release locally; refuses in cluster, foreground and concurrent-update cases; and adds `--override-quarantine`.

The rollback implementation is not in this batch, so the following contracts are unverified. They touch T-043 (the watchdog and rollback authority is the same replaceable binary), T-013, T-054 and TB-009/TB-011.

- The kept release's integrity and signature check, and its binding to the installed-bundle record.
- Whether the kept release is still a qualified, non-revoked App Attest build. The docs say rollback contacts no coordinator, so a revoked or deactivated build could be restored locally. Serving would still require runtime Apple proof and coordinator authorization (A-016/A-017, T-054), so the coordinator remains the enforcement point. This is a design question for the implementation review, not a defect shown here.
- Whether the downgrade bypass of the updater's never-install-older rule is limited to the single recorded kept bundle. The kept bundle needs owner-only storage so a local same-UID actor cannot swap it.
- Whether the quarantine record tamper-resists, and whether the interactive confirmation and `--yes` cannot be driven by an unprivileged local process into a downgrade to a known-vulnerable release.

The next review pass should examine the Swift update/rollback code and the watchdog for these contracts. The doc statement that deactivation does not remove a bad release from a Mac is accurate to existing behavior and is not a new exposure.
